metadata.title: Create-Viz Isn't About Making It Pretty.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: when Claude 'creates a visualization,' does it make the chart pretty, or does it pick the right chart type and keep the axis honest first? Lands the carry-out that style comes after accuracy, never instead of it.
metadata.anchor_pair: N/A — source is skill-teardown format (anatomy -> pipeline -> constraint -> verdict), no anchor structure to preserve

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes this skill's whole job is making a chart look pretty. It isn't — it's a decision procedure: which chart type fits the data, and rules that keep the chart honest, before anything gets styled.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude, make my chart pretty.', hesitates on 'pretty', corrects to 'honest'

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 35-word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('pretty'->'honest') is visible on a late frame.

beats.act: 1 anatomy — a skill is a folder
beats.narration_text: This kind of work runs on something called a skill — a folder Claude reads before it acts. Inside, one file spells out how a query result or a pasted table becomes a chart: read the request, load the data, pick a chart type, write the code, then save and hand it back. The file is the whole program.

shot.new_visual_element: A folder icon opening to reveal SKILL.md, reference/gotchas.md, reference/examples/; SKILL.md highlighted

production_viz.label: A skill is a folder
production_viz.mechanic: A folder opens on cream to reveal three items: SKILL.md (highlighted in crimson), reference/gotchas.md, reference/examples/. A caption below reads 'Claude reads it, then follows it.'

beats.narration_text: Before any styling, it matches chart to relationship: a trend over time gets a line, a comparison across categories gets a bar, a part of a whole gets a stacked bar, a distribution gets a histogram, two variables that move together get a scatter plot. The type comes from what the data is doing, not from what looks nice.

shot.new_visual_element: A relationship-to-chart-type table filling in row by row: trend->line, comparison->bar, part-to-whole->stacked bar, distribution->histogram, correlation->scatter

production_viz.label: Relationship decides the chart
production_viz.mechanic: A two-column table fills in one row at a time on cream: 'Trend over time -> Line', 'Comparison -> Bar', 'Part-to-whole -> Stacked bar', 'Distribution -> Histogram', 'Correlation -> Scatter'. The last row is boxed in crimson.

beats.narration_text: And it won't style around the truth. Bar charts have to start at zero. Axis breaks can't hide the size of a change. Colors have to be readable by someone colorblind, and they mean something — they don't just decorate. A title has to state the actual finding, not just name the numbers. Pretty was never the first requirement; honest was.

shot.new_visual_element: A bar chart forced to a zero baseline; a colorblind-safe palette swatch; a title reading an actual finding instead of a metric name

production_viz.label: Accuracy, not decoration
production_viz.mechanic: A bar chart's baseline snaps down to zero when a ghost bar tries to float above it. Beside it, a colorblind-safe swatch row locks in. Below both, a title card swaps from 'Revenue by Month' to 'Revenue grew 23% YoY', the second one boxed in crimson. Footer: 'Pretty was never the first requirement.'

beats.narration_text: Create-viz doesn't start by making a chart pretty — it starts by matching the chart type to what the data actually shows. Style comes after accuracy, never instead of it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Here's some made-up monthly revenue for six months. Before you make this pretty, tell me what chart type it calls for and why, then build it with the axis kept honest. Liam, in for Bear.
